summaryEn: Taiwan's vertically integrated chicken business — feed mills, farms, slaughterhouses and branded frozen food under one roof. It earned a record NT$10.40 per share in 2025, then watched profit halve in a single quarter when a Middle East conflict sent oil, freight and grain prices up together.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + company earnings call; poultry framing — the vertical integration, record FY2025 (gross margin 21.2% vs 16.4%, net profit +62%) and 24.9% ROE credited, but the 2026Q1 reversal stated in full with the company's own verified attribution (oil US$70→110-120, freight +30-50%, grain squeezed, only NT$0.5 of feed price passed through), and the 66.1% debt ratio against NT$364m of cash flagged; every FinMind figure cross-checked against company disclosure; sector Food & Beverage → Poultry & Animal Feed)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Charoen Pokphand Enterprise (卜蜂企業, TWSE: 1215) is Taiwan's most vertically integrated protein business. Founded in **1977** and **listed in July 1987**, it operates the entire chain: **feed mills, broiler and pig farming, slaughtering and processing, branded chilled and frozen foods, and foodservice supply**. It is the Taiwanese arm of the **Charoen Pokphand** group of Thailand, one of the world's largest agri-food companies.

Vertical integration is the whole strategy. Feed is roughly **70% of the cost of raising a chicken**, so a company that both mills the feed and raises the birds captures margin at two stages and can manage the relationship between them. Feed alone is a brutal business — **gross margins of 3–4% and net margins under 3%** — but branded chilled and frozen chicken sold to supermarkets and restaurant chains earns considerably more. Moving volume up that chain is how the company makes money.

**FY2025 was the best year in its history.** Gross margin reached **21.2% against 16.4% in 2024**, net profit rose **62% to NT$3.07bn**, and EPS hit **NT$10.40** — up from NT$6.55. Trailing **return on equity is 24.91%**, among the highest in this collection, and the dividend was raised to **NT$7.0**, giving a **6.60% yield** at NT$106.00 on **11.4× earnings**.

**Then the first quarter of 2026 halved it.** Revenue rose **7.1% to NT$7.17bn** — but **net profit fell 47.1% and EPS came in at NT$1.26**, against NT$2.38 a year earlier. Gross margin dropped from **21.4% to 17.8%** and operating margin from **13.8% to 8.0%**. The company's own explanation is specific: **a Middle East conflict in late February pushed oil from about US$70 to US$110–120 a barrel**, freight costs rose **30–50%**, and **corn and soybean supply was squeezed**, lifting feed raw-material prices. The company raised feed prices by **NT$0.5** but could not fully pass the increase through.

That is the essential nature of this business, stated plainly: **revenue can grow while profit halves**, because the cost of the primary input is set in global commodity markets and the selling price is not. The balance sheet reflects an agricultural operation — **NT$32.5bn of assets on NT$11.0bn of equity, a 66.1% debt ratio, and just NT$364m of cash** — though **operating cash flow of NT$946m comfortably exceeded NT$373m of net income** in the weak quarter.

The honest read: **an excellent, genuinely integrated protein operator earning a 25% return on equity — whose margin is a spread between two prices it does not control, as one quarter has just demonstrated.**

The company was established in **1977** as the Taiwanese operation of **Charoen Pokphand**, the Thai conglomerate founded by the Chearavanont family that grew from a seed shop into one of the world's largest agri-food businesses. CP's model, replicated across Asia, was **vertical integration in protein**: mill the feed, breed and raise the animals, slaughter and process them, and sell the finished product under a brand.

The logic is economic rather than ideological. **Feed accounts for roughly 70% of the cost of producing a chicken**, and feed itself is a **3–4% gross margin business** dominated by the price of corn and soybean meal. A pure feed miller is therefore permanently exposed to commodity swings with almost no cushion. A pure poultry farmer buying feed on the open market is exposed to the same swings from the other side. **A company that does both internalises the largest cost relationship in the industry** — and if it also processes and brands the meat, it captures the higher margin at the consumer end.

Taiwan turned out to be a good market for this. The island's consumers shifted toward chilled and processed poultry, supermarket and convenience-store channels grew, and restaurant chains needed reliable, food-safety-assured supply. CP Taiwan built out the **branded chilled and frozen food business** and **foodservice supply** to capture that shift, moving progressively away from being a feed company that also raised chickens. It **listed in 1987**.

The strategy's payoff arrived in **FY2025**, the best year in the company's history: **gross margin of 21.2% against 16.4% the year before**, net profit up **62%**, and **EPS of NT$10.40** — the product of favourable feed costs meeting a stronger product mix.

Its limits arrived one quarter later. In **2026Q1**, a **Middle East conflict lifted oil from about US$70 to US$110–120**, freight rose **30–50%**, and grain supply tightened. Vertical integration means owning both sides of a spread — which is a strength when input costs fall and an exposure when they rise faster than prices can be raised.

- **1977 (22 Aug)** — Founded as the Taiwanese operation of Thailand's **Charoen Pokphand** group.
- **1987 (27 July)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (1215)**.
- **1990s–2010s** — Builds the integrated chain: **feed mills, broiler and pig farming, slaughter and processing**, then **branded chilled and frozen foods** and **foodservice supply**.
- **2019–2021** — Dividends of **NT$4.0**, **NT$4.5** and **NT$3.0**.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$5.55**; dividend NT$3.5.
- **2023** — **FY2023 EPS NT$7.70**; dividend raised to **NT$5.5**.
- **2024** — A weaker year: **FY2024 EPS NT$6.55**, gross margin **16.4%**; dividend **NT$4.5**.
- **2025** — **A record year.** Gross margin rises to **21.2%**, net profit **+62% to NT$3.07bn**, **EPS NT$10.40**; quarterly EPS runs **2.38, 2.58, 2.99, 2.45**. Dividend raised to **NT$7.0**.
- **2026 (late February)** — A **Middle East conflict** pushes oil from about **US$70 to US$110–120** a barrel; freight costs rise **30–50%**; corn and soybean supply is squeezed.
- **2026Q1** — **Revenue NT$7.17bn (+7.1%) but net profit −47.1% and EPS NT$1.26.** Gross margin falls **21.4% → 17.8%**, operating margin **13.8% → 8.0%**. The company raises feed prices **NT$0.5** without fully recovering costs.

CP Taiwan's accounts show **a high-return integrated operator whose margin is a commodity spread**.

- **A record year, then a halving.** Annual EPS: **NT$5.55 (FY2022) → 7.70 (FY2023) → 6.55 (FY2024) → NT$10.40 (FY2025)**. FY2025 gross margin reached **21.2% against 16.4% in FY2024**, and net profit rose **62% to NT$3.07bn**. Then **2026Q1 EPS came in at NT$1.26 against NT$2.38** — a **47.1% fall in net profit on 7.1% revenue growth**.
- **The cause is documented and external.** Per the company's own account: a **late-February Middle East conflict** lifted oil from about **US$70 to US$110–120 a barrel**, **freight costs rose 30–50%**, and **corn and soybean supply was squeezed**, raising feed raw-material costs. The company **raised feed prices by NT$0.5** but could not fully pass the increase through. Margins compressed accordingly: gross **21.4% → 17.8%**, operating **13.8% → 8.0%**, net **10.4% → 5.2%**.
- **Return on equity is exceptional — and leverage contributes.** **24.91% trailing**, on equity of only **NT$11.0bn** supporting **NT$32.5bn of assets**. A **66.1% debt ratio** amplifies both good years and bad ones.
- **Cash is thin, but cash flow is not.** The balance sheet holds just **NT$364m of cash**. However, **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$946m was more than 2.5× net income of NT$373m** — agricultural operations turn inventory quickly, and the working-capital cycle is favourable.
- **A dividend raised on a record year.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$4.0 (2019) → 4.5 → 3.0 → 3.5 (2022) → 5.5 (2023) → 4.5 (2024) → NT$7.0 (2025)**. Against FY2025 EPS of **NT$10.40** that is a **67% payout**, giving a **6.60% yield** at NT$106.00. The record also shows the payout following earnings both ways — **NT$3.0 in 2021, NT$7.0 in 2025**.
- **Valuation.** **11.4× earnings and 2.95× book.** The low P/E reflects a record trailing year; the high price-to-book reflects the high return on a small equity base.

The financing reality: **outstanding returns generated with meaningful leverage on a thin equity base, from a margin that global commodity prices can compress in a single quarter.**

**Stance: Taiwan's best-integrated protein business, earning 24.9% on equity with a 6.60% yield after a record year — whose profit halved in one quarter when oil, freight and grain rose together.**

The bull case:

1. **Genuine vertical integration in the right places.** **Feed is ~70% of the cost of a chicken**, and CP Taiwan mills its own — then raises, slaughters, processes and brands. That converts a **3–4% gross margin feed business** into a company earning **21.2% gross margin** in a good year.
2. **A record demonstrated the model works.** FY2025 gross margin **21.2% against 16.4%**, net profit **+62% to NT$3.07bn**, **EPS NT$10.40**, and **24.91% return on equity**.
3. **Real income.** A **6.60% yield** on a **67% payout**, at **11.4× earnings**, with **operating cash flow more than 2.5× net income** even in a weak quarter.
4. **Structural demand.** Taiwanese consumption continues shifting toward **chilled, processed and food-safety-assured protein** through supermarkets, convenience stores and restaurant chains — the higher-margin end of the chain.

The counter-arguments:

- **The margin is a spread between two prices the company does not set.** **2026Q1 proved it: revenue +7.1%, net profit −47.1%.** Feed grain and freight are global commodities; retail chicken prices are not adjusted weekly.
- **Leverage amplifies both directions.** **66.1% debt ratio** on **NT$11.0bn of equity**, with only **NT$364m of cash**. The 24.9% ROE partly reflects that leverage.
- **The dividend follows earnings.** **NT$7.0 for FY2025** came after **NT$4.5** and **NT$3.0** in earlier years. The **6.60% yield** is a record year's yield.
- **Disease and regulatory risk.** Poultry and pig operations carry avian influenza and African swine fever exposure, which can halt production or trade without warning.

A **commodity-spread** thesis: an excellent operator of a genuinely integrated chain — bought with the understanding that one geopolitical event can halve a quarter.

CP Taiwan makes money by **owning every step between a grain of corn and a packaged chicken breast**:

- **Feed milling (the base, and the thin part).** Corn and soybean meal are milled into compound feed for poultry, pigs and aquaculture. On its own this is a **3–4% gross margin business with net margins under 3%** — it exists to feed the company's own animals and to sell to external farmers, not to generate profit by itself.
- **Farming.** Broiler chickens and pigs, raised on the company's own feed. Because **feed is roughly 70% of the cost of raising a bird**, controlling the feed controls the dominant cost — and removes the margin an external supplier would take.
- **Slaughter and processing.** Converting live animals into chilled, frozen and further-processed products under controlled, traceable conditions — increasingly what Taiwanese retailers and restaurant chains require.
- **Branded foods and foodservice.** Chilled and frozen chicken and prepared products sold under the **卜蜂 brand** through supermarkets and convenience stores, plus bulk supply to restaurant chains. **This is where the margin is**, and moving volume here is the strategic priority.
- **Why the margin swings so hard.** Revenue is roughly **grain cost plus a spread**. When grain and freight fall, the spread widens and profit surges — FY2025's **21.2% gross margin against 16.4%**. When they rise faster than selling prices can follow, the spread collapses — **2026Q1's 17.8% gross margin and 47.1% profit decline on 7.1% revenue growth**. The company raised feed prices **NT$0.5** and still could not recover the increase.

The levers are **grain and freight costs, chicken and pork prices, product mix (branded versus commodity), and how quickly price increases can be passed through**. The strength is that integration captures margin at several stages and gives control over the largest cost. The vulnerability is that **integration does not create pricing power over inputs** — it internalises the exposure rather than removing it, on a balance sheet carrying a **66.1% debt ratio** and **NT$364m of cash**.

Protein production is an industry where the winners are integrated and the margins are spreads.

- **Why integration dominates globally.** Companies like **Tyson, JBS, BRF and Charoen Pokphand** grew by controlling feed, farming and processing together. The reason is structural: feed is the dominant cost, animal biology sets the production cycle, and food safety requires traceability. **An integrator manages all three; a specialist at any one stage is a price-taker at the others.**
- **The Taiwanese market.** CP Taiwan competes with **Great Wall (大成長城, 1210)** — also in this collection — and with **Charoen Pokphand's own regional operations**, plus smaller feed millers and independent farmers. Great Wall is stronger in feed and flour; CP Taiwan is more weighted toward integrated poultry and branded food. Both benefit from the same shift toward chilled, packaged and traceable protein.
- **What determines industry profitability.** Two commodity prices: **corn and soybean meal on the cost side**, and **chicken and pork prices on the revenue side**. Both are set by global harvests, energy costs, freight and disease outbreaks. **2026Q1 was a textbook case** — an oil price shock raised freight **30–50%** and squeezed grain supply simultaneously, compressing the spread from both directions.
- **Consumer trends favour the integrated.** Taiwanese demand has moved from wet-market fresh poultry toward **chilled, packaged, brand-assured product** sold through supermarkets and convenience stores, and toward **restaurant chains** requiring consistent specification. Both channels reward scale, food-safety systems and traceability — which is exactly what integration provides.
- **The tail risks are biological.** **Avian influenza** and **African swine fever** can halt production, close export markets or force culls with no warning. This is a permanent feature of the industry, not an occasional event.

CP Taiwan's position is **strong within its structure**. The industry truth is that **integration determines who survives the cycles, not whether the cycles happen** — profitability remains a spread between global grain and local meat prices, and no amount of operational excellence changes that.

**Strengths**
- **Full vertical integration**: feed mills, farming, slaughter, processing, branded foods and foodservice.
- **Record FY2025**: gross margin **21.2%** (from 16.4%), net profit **+62% to NT$3.07bn**, **EPS NT$10.40**.
- **24.91% trailing return on equity**; **operating cash flow more than 2.5× net income** even in a weak quarter.
- **6.60% dividend yield** on a **67% payout**, at **11.4× earnings**.

**Weaknesses**
- **Margin is a commodity spread**: 2026Q1 revenue **+7.1%** but net profit **−47.1%**.
- **66.1% debt ratio** on **NT$11.0bn of equity**, with only **NT$364m of cash**.
- **Feed alone earns 3–4% gross margin**; pass-through of cost increases is slow.
- The dividend follows earnings — **NT$3.0 (2021) to NT$7.0 (2025)**.

**Opportunities**
- Continued consumer shift toward **chilled, branded, traceable protein** and restaurant-chain supply.
- Mix shift further toward processed and branded products.
- Normalisation of oil, freight and grain costs restoring the spread.

**Threats**
- **Grain and freight cost shocks** — as the late-February oil move demonstrated.
- **Avian influenza and African swine fever** halting production or trade.
- Retail price resistance limiting pass-through of input costs.

- **Input costs can halve profit in one quarter (demonstrated, not hypothetical).** In **2026Q1 revenue rose 7.1% while net profit fell 47.1%**. The company's stated cause: a **late-February Middle East conflict** taking oil from about **US$70 to US$110–120**, freight up **30–50%**, and corn and soybean supply squeezed. A **NT$0.5 feed price increase** did not recover it. Grain and energy are global commodities; Taiwanese retail meat prices adjust slowly.
- **Leverage amplifies the swing.** A **66.1% debt ratio** on **NT$11.0bn of equity** supporting **NT$32.5bn of assets**, with only **NT$364m of cash**. The **24.91% return on equity** is genuinely good — and partly a function of that leverage, which works equally hard in reverse.
- **The trailing figures are a record.** FY2025's **NT$10.40 EPS** and **21.2% gross margin** were the best in the company's history, achieved when input costs were favourable. Valuing the company on **11.4× earnings** uses that record year as the base.
- **The dividend is not fixed.** **NT$7.0 for FY2025** followed **NT$4.5** and **NT$3.0**. The **6.60% yield** reflects a record payout on record earnings; both move with the spread.
- **Biological risk.** **Avian influenza** in poultry and **African swine fever** in pigs can force culls, close markets and halt processing. Integration concentrates this risk rather than diversifying it — an outbreak affects farming, processing and branded supply simultaneously.
- **Pass-through lag.** Retail and foodservice contracts do not reprice weekly. Even when the company can eventually raise prices, the gap between a cost increase and a price increase falls entirely on the margin.

CP Taiwan's outlook depends on **whether the input-cost shock reverses and how much of it can be passed on.** The axes to watch:

- **Gross margin — the spread itself.** It ran **16.4% (FY2024) → 21.2% (FY2025) → 17.8% (2026Q1)**. Recovery toward 21% would mean grain and freight normalised or prices were successfully raised; continued compression means the shock is persisting.
- **Grain and freight costs.** The direct driver. Oil at **US$110–120** versus **US$70**, and freight **30–50% higher**, are external conditions the company can only respond to. Their direction sets the year.
- **Price pass-through.** The company raised feed prices **NT$0.5** without full recovery. How much more it can pass to farmers, retailers and restaurant chains — and how quickly — determines how much of the shock lands on shareholders.
- **Mix.** The share of **branded chilled, frozen and processed products** versus commodity feed and live animals. A richer mix structurally widens the spread and reduces sensitivity.
- **The dividend.** **NT$7.0 for FY2025** at a **67% payout**. If FY2026 earnings fall materially from **NT$10.40**, the payout will follow — as it has before.

Bottom line: CP Taiwan runs **the most complete protein chain in Taiwan** — feed, farms, slaughter, processing and brands — and in **FY2025 turned that into a record: 21.2% gross margin, net profit up 62%, EPS NT$10.40, and a 24.91% return on equity**, paying **NT$7.0** for a **6.60% yield**. It then showed the other side of the model in a single quarter: **revenue up 7.1%, profit down 47.1%**, when oil, freight and grain all moved against it at once, on a balance sheet carrying a **66.1% debt ratio** and **NT$364m of cash**. Judge it on **gross margin and input costs** — an excellent integrator operating a spread it does not control.
